As of 335 AM EST Monday...

KEY MESSAGE 1...Unseasonably warm today ahead of a strong cold 
frontal passage.

Coastal low pressure has lifted well north and east of the area and 
is centered near the New England coast as of this writing. Low 
stratus and areas of fog are in place across most of the area 
as low level moisture remains locked in over the region in the 
wake low pressure and rainfall yesterday. It will take some time
after sunrise for this low level moisture to mix out, 
especially across SE portions of the area. A strong cold front 
approaches from the west this morning and crosses the area this 
afternoon into the evening hours. We should improve to partly 
cloudy conditions by this afternoon with temperatures forecast 
to rise well above seasonal norms for late November. Afternoon 
high temps will be in the low 70s for most of the area with some
mid and upper 60s expected on the Eastern Shore. CAM guidance 
continues to show the potential for showers along as well as in 
the wake of the front. QPF will generally be light with this 
activity but some meager instability (on the order of 250 J/kg) 
may allow for some localized higher rainfall totals. Strong cold
advection and deep mixing will allow winds to remain breezy 
inland overnight, even more so at the coast. Lows tonight dip 
into the mid 30s NW with upper 30s and low 40s for the remainder
of the area. Mid and upper 40s are forecast from Hampton Roads 
southward into northeastern NC. 

Much cooler Tuesday with mostly sunny skies. Highs top out in the 
50s with overnight lows in the upper 20s NW to the upper 30s and low 
40s SE.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Confidence continues to increase regarding an 
impactful storm across the region late Wednesday into 
Thanksgiving Day with the potential for heavy rainfall and gusty
winds. 

00z guidance remains in excellent agreement showing strong high 
pressure (1040+mb) setting up over New England on Wednesday with low 
pressure developing off the Southeast coast. This low is forecast to 
lift northward through the afternoon into the overnight period, 
setting up a strong pressure gradient over the area. NE winds will 
strengthen through the day and into the overnight, especially at the 
coast. Low level moisture increases as well with PoPs increasing 
across the south in the afternoon, spreading northward after sunset. 
There remains some disagreement on the complex upper level pattern 
between the GFS/ECMWF and its impact on surface low track and 
strength. The ECMWF shows a potent, negatively-tilted southern 
stream trough and a stronger surface low than the GFS but both 
eventually show phasing of the northern and southern stream 
jets. Regardless of the finer details, confidence continues to 
increase that beneficial moderate to locally heavy rainfall will
move into the area late Wednesday night and Thursday. 
Probabilities for >2" of QPF have increased 50-70% on the EPS 
while the GEFS shows 20-40%. Each ensemble favors the eastern 
half of the area for the heaviest QPF but both show widespread 
60-90% probs for >1". Gusty winds are likely area-wide Wednesday
night and especially on Thursday as low pressure lifts 
northward across the region. Gusts inland are forecast to be in 
the 25-40mph range with gusts near the coast 30-45mph. 
Depending on the exact strength of the surface low, gusts of 
40-50mph are possible at the coast on Thursday. Precip will end 
from south to north Thursday evening as low pressure lifts north
of the area. 

With many folks likely to be traveling during the peak impacts from 
this system, users should closely monitor the forecast over the next 
24-36 hours as details come into focus.


KEY MESSAGE 3...Widespread moderate to major coastal flooding is 
becoming increasingly likely Wednesday night into Friday.

Confidence continues to increase in a significant coastal flooding 
event, starting as soon as Wednesday night and continuing into 
Friday as strong and prolonged onshore winds associated with a 
developing low pressure system coincide with astronomical tides. The 
ongoing King Tide cycle, full moon, and lunar perigee will result in 
unusually high astronomical tides, increasing the potential for 
substantial coastal flooding as tidal departures rise ahead of the 
system. Latest guidance continues to favor a strong area of high 
pressure over New England and developing low pressure tracking N to 
NW towards the region Wednesday into Thursday. This setup supports 
an extended period of E-NE winds, with winds potentially becoming E-
SE as the low tracks inland on Thursday. Winds then snap back to the 
W-SW later Thursday into Friday as the system departs. The duration 
and orientation of the initial onshore flow will be critical in 
determining the exact magnitude and locations of coastal flooding. 

The current forecast follows the P-ETSS mean closely, which supports 
widespread moderate flooding. However, major flooding is forecast is
